card: No alliance obliges you, yet the responsibility is yours. When, and to whom, will you show your hand?
intro: You are Sir Edward Grey, who has run Britain’s foreign policy since December 1905. Britain has ententes with France and Russia, but no treaty obliges it to fight beside them, and the decision for war rests with the Cabinet and Parliament. By Churchill’s later account, at least three-quarters of the Cabinet are determined to keep out of a European quarrel unless Britain itself is attacked, and Prime Minister Asquith fears that Irish Home Rule will bring civil war. Around you are Nicolson and Crowe at the Foreign Office, who believe in the friendship with France; Churchill, the ardent First Lord of the Admiralty; and Lloyd George, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, weighing the peace party against the interventionists. In London the sharp French ambassador, Paul Cambon, and the anglophile German ambassador, Lichnowsky, are waiting on your word. Behind you stand the largest fleet in the world and the influence that comes with being British foreign secretary.

GB-00.title: News from Sarajevo

telegram.text: Vice-Consul at Sarajevo telegraphs Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Duchess of Hohenberg assassinated / Another source: bomb first thrown at their car on way to town hall; on return young Serbian student shot them both with a revolver

GB-00.event: On the morning of Sunday, 28 June, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife were assassinated in Sarajevo, Bosnia.
GB-00.scene: London first heard the news at 4 p.m. on Sunday, 28 June, from the consul at Sarajevo; at 6 p.m. a telegram from Ambassador de Bunsen in Vienna gave the details. That same day a British squadron was being entertained by the German navy at Kiel, and Wilhelm II cut short his program and returned to Berlin when he heard. King George V ordered a week of court mourning. On the afternoon of 30 June, Prime Minister Asquith moved a resolution in the Commons conveying condolences to the Austrian emperor, and Bonar Law, the Conservative leader, seconded it. The archduke and his wife had been the King’s guests at Windsor Castle the previous November. The same day you told the House, in answer to a question, that the Dardanelles had not been discussed with Russia at any time in the past five years.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, moving the resolution of condolence in the Commons, 30 June)
voices.text: Mr. Speaker, we are once more confronted with one of those incredible crimes which almost make us despair of the progress of mankind.

voices.who: Grey (you, private letter to Ambassador Mensdorff, 29 June)
voices.text: His life is so bound up with the peace of Europe that I dread anything that must try his strength.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: It is a terrible crime, but I doubt it will have serious political consequences beyond Austria-Hungary. The Vienna papers will attack Serbia fiercely, but it is not for Britain to step forward.

choices.text: Have Crackanthorpe at the Belgrade legation advise Serbia early to cooperate fully in any inquiry into the plot
choices.why: If Serbia shows good faith first, Vienna has fewer pretexts left
choices.after: The Serbian government replied that it would cooperate as far as its laws allowed, but the Vienna papers branded the whole Serbian government an accomplice. British advice drew little response in either Belgrade or Vienna.

choices.text: Through the Berlin embassy, privately ask the German Foreign Office to join Britain in keeping Vienna from going too far
choices.why: Only Germany can stop Vienna, so bring Berlin in early
choices.after: Ambassador Lichnowsky was on leave in Germany, and the German Foreign Office sent only a polite reply. London did not know that at Potsdam on 5 and 6 July Germany had already promised Austria its unconditional support.

choices.text: Send condolences to Vienna and support the Commons resolution; leave the inquiry and its handling to Vienna and watch
choices.why: Meddling too soon in another country’s tragedy only invites suspicion
choices.after: On 29 June you telegraphed Vienna to convey the government’s deep sympathy, and the Commons resolution passed without dissent. The world’s sympathy lay with Austria, and for the first weeks the attitude of the government in Vienna seemed neither extreme nor alarmist.

note.text: In June 1914 the Royal Navy visited Russia’s Kronstadt and then Germany’s Kiel, showing goodwill to both. The British embassy in Berlin reported that the Kiel visit had gone well, though part of the program on the last day was canceled after the news from Sarajevo.

map.caption: The news from Sarajevo reached London by way of Vienna on 28 June. That month the Royal Navy visited Kronstadt and then Kiel.

GB-00a.title: Questions About the Naval Talks
GB-00a.event: On 6 July the German ambassador, Lichnowsky, back from Berlin, called privately to tell you that Austria meant to do something about Serbia and that military action could not be ruled out.
GB-00a.scene: On Monday, Lichnowsky had poured out the anxiety and pessimism he had found in Berlin: Austria intended to act against Serbia, Russia was arming, and Berlin suspected that Britain and Russia had a naval agreement. In fact the two navies had been holding talks since May with the Cabinet’s permission, and their substance had leaked to Berlin through an informant inside the Russian embassy. On 11 June you told the Commons that no such negotiations were in progress; Berlin officially accepted that answer but still suspects some arrangement between the two navies. Today you sit down with Lichnowsky again to give him the answer you put off on Monday.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist of the 6 July conversation as Grey recorded it)
voices.text: Some in Germany feel that trouble is bound to come anyway, so it would be better not to restrain Austria and to let the trouble come now rather than later.

voices.who: Grey (you, answer in the Commons, 11 June)
voices.text: No such negotiations are in progress, and none are likely to be entered upon, as far as I can judge.

voices.who: Benckendorff (Russian ambassador in London, gist of the 8 July conversation)
voices.text: It is true that the Russian army has grown and is better prepared for war. So some in Germany may think it better to clash early, before the odds get worse. I can only hope that Germany will restrain Austria.

choices.text: Take Berlin’s anxieties seriously and tell Lichnowsky the naval talks with Russia will be suspended for the time being
choices.why: Easing Berlin’s fear of encirclement gives Britain the leverage to restrain Vienna
choices.after: Lichnowsky was delighted and telegraphed Berlin that same day that Britain had shown goodwill. But the next day Benckendorff came to the Foreign Office to protest that Britain had dropped, at a word from Germany, talks Russia had obtained with difficulty through France.

choices.text: Admit to military talks since 1906 but say the government’s hands are free, and pledge to work for peace as in the Balkan crisis
choices.why: Hide nothing and promise nothing, and both sides will go on trusting you
choices.after: You said that there had been conversations between the military and naval authorities since 1906, but that the government’s hands had always been free, and that any agreement imposing obligations would not be made in secret but laid before Parliament. You promised that the greater the risk of war, the more firmly you would hold to the policy of the Balkan crisis. Lichnowsky said he hoped the German government had moderated Austria’s intentions, but he knew nothing more himself.

choices.text: Repeat the 11 June answer to the Commons word for word, and say nothing has passed between the two countries' naval authorities
choices.why: Contradicting what was said in Parliament would only make matters worse
choices.after: Lichnowsky listened politely, but Berlin did not believe it. The German Foreign Office already had the substance of the naval talks in hand, and from then on it would not take the British foreign secretary’s word at face value.

note.text: In April 1914 Grey accompanied King George V to Paris and discussed the matter with Prime Minister Doumergue; in May the Cabinet allowed British–Russian naval talks only within the terms of the 1912 Grey–Cambon letters. On 25 June Grey told Benckendorff he was concerned that figures such as Germany’s Theodor Schiemann were getting information about a naval agreement from acquaintances in Paris and St Petersburg.

pressure.title: Your Answer to Parliament
pressure.text: When a question was put in the Commons on 11 June about a naval agreement between Britain and Russia, you answered that no such negotiations were in progress. In your later memoir you would admit that, while the answer was true, there was no denying the criticism that it did not answer the question put to you. Your view is that Parliament has a right to know of any agreement that binds the country, but not of the military and naval preparations made against the possibility of war.

GB-00b.title: The Price of Halting the Talks
GB-00b.scene: Your word that the naval talks would stop reassured Berlin a little, but in St Petersburg Sazonov began to suspect that Britain was leaning toward Germany. Ambassador Buchanan reported that Russian newspapers were attacking the entente with Britain as weaker than the German–Austrian alliance. From Vienna, Ambassador de Bunsen reported a growing feeling, centered on the military, that this time the account with Serbia must be settled. You must decide what to do with the trust you have won in Berlin.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Berlin appreciates Britain’s goodwill. If London and Berlin speak together, Vienna will not be able to go too far.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: If we lose Russia’s trust, we will pay for it in Persia and on the Indian frontier. Russia’s friendship matters more to Britain than Germany’s goodwill.

choices.text: Take up Lichnowsky’s idea of a joint London–Berlin line and write privately to Bethmann Hollweg proposing to restrain Vienna
choices.why: Trust won in Berlin is worth something only if it is spent restraining Vienna
choices.after: Bethmann Hollweg replied that he respected Britain’s wishes, but he did not reveal that on 5 and 6 July Germany had already promised Austria its unconditional support. Meanwhile, in Vienna, the note to Serbia was quietly being polished.

choices.text: Follow Nicolson’s warning: call in Benckendorff and promise that the naval talks with Russia will resume in the autumn
choices.why: With Persia and India in mind, Russia’s friendship has to come first
choices.after: Benckendorff was relieved, but this promise also soon leaked to Berlin. The German Foreign Office concluded that British promises did not last more than a few days and trusted London’s word even less.

note.text: Even after the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 the two countries often clashed in Persia, and in June and July 1914 Grey’s Foreign Office was in serious negotiations with Russia over Persia and Tibet.

GB-01.title: Fermanagh and Tyrone
GB-01.clock: About 26 hours until the deadline for Serbia’s reply (6 p.m. on 25 July, Belgrade time)

telegram.from: Foreign Office (delivered by the Austro-Hungarian embassy)
telegram.text: Austria-Hungary delivered note at Belgrade 6 p.m. 23 July / 48-hour time limit for reply / Demands include participation of Austrian officials in suppressing anti-Austrian movement

GB-01.event: At 6 p.m. on 23 July the Austrian minister, Giesl, handed the Serbian government a note with a 48-hour time limit.
GB-01.scene: The Cabinet, which met at 3:15 p.m., has been taken up with Ireland from the start. The Buckingham Palace Conference on Ireland that King George V had called (21–24 July) broke down today, and ministers trudge on through the long argument over which parishes of the two counties of Fermanagh and Tyrone to leave out of Home Rule. Only yesterday, Chancellor of the Exchequer Lloyd George had told the Commons that relations with Germany were very much better than they had been a few years earlier. As the meeting draws to a close, you begin to read out, in a low, even voice, a document sent over from the Foreign Office: the note Austria-Hungary handed to Belgrade yesterday evening.

voices.who: Grey (you, to the Austrian ambassador Mensdorff that morning)
voices.text: I had never before seen one State address to another independent State a document of so formidable a character.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, in his later memoir)
voices.text: The parishes of Fermanagh and Tyrone faded back into the mists and squalls of Ireland, and a strange light began immediately, but by perceptible gradations, to fall and grow upon the map of Europe.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, letter to Venetia Stanley that day)
voices.text: We are within measurable, or imaginable, distance of a real Armageddon. (…) Happily there seems to be no reason why we should be anything more than spectators.

choices.text: Propose that Britain, Germany, France and Italy mediate between Vienna and St Petersburg, keeping Britain’s own position open
choices.why: Only four powers with no direct stake can let both sides save face
choices.after: That day you put the four-power mediation plan to Cambon and Lichnowsky. Cambon countered that once Austria attacked Serbia, Russian opinion would boil over and mediation would come too late. Britain still stood with neither side.

choices.text: Hold mediation in reserve until Austria and Russia face each other directly, and let the Cabinet focus on the failed Irish talks
choices.why: Civil war in Ireland is a nearer danger than a quarrel in the Balkans
choices.after: Ministers went back to the map of Ulster with relief. But at the French Foreign Ministry in Paris, officials began to worry that Britain regarded this crisis as someone else’s business.

choices.text: Call in Lichnowsky and warn him first: if an Austro-Russian clash becomes a European war, Britain will find it hard to stand aside
choices.why: Germany will not restrain Vienna while it trusts in British neutrality
choices.after: Lichnowsky passed the warning straight to Berlin, but the German Foreign Office took it as the usual British vagueness. The Cabinet’s non-interventionists complained that you had gone ahead without any mandate.

note.text: The Parliament Act of 1911 limited the House of Lords to delaying a bill for two years, and in May 1914 the Home Rule Bill passed the Commons for the third time and awaited enactment. Ulster’s Protestants had formed the Ulster Volunteer Force in 1913, and in April 1914 they smuggled about 25,000 rifles, bought from an arms dealer in Hamburg, into Larne and other Ulster ports; throughout July Britain feared civil war.

pressure.title: Ireland on the Brink of Civil War
pressure.text: On 20 March at the Curragh camp, Brigadier-General Gough and 57 officers of the cavalry brigade declared that they would rather accept dismissal than be sent against Ulster; the affair forced out War Secretary Seely and the Chief of the Imperial General Staff, French, and Asquith took over the War Office himself. In April the Ulster Volunteers smuggled about 25,000 rifles into Larne and other ports, and the Buckingham Palace Conference called by the King broke down on 24 July. If this Cabinet splits again over Europe, the government and any settlement of the Irish question may fall together.

GB-02.title: A Declaration of Solidarity
GB-02.clock: About 8 hours until the deadline for Serbia’s reply

telegram.text: Foreign Minister Sazonov and French ambassador ask for British declaration of solidarity / France will fulfill obligations of alliance / I replied, speaking personally, that unconditional declaration of support could hardly be expected

GB-02.scene: On Saturday morning the summer trees of St James’s Park fill the view from your office window. On your desk lies the telegram Ambassador Buchanan sent overnight from St Petersburg, and Assistant Under-Secretary Crowe has added a long minute to it. Russian Foreign Minister Sazonov and the French ambassador, Paléologue, are asking Britain to declare that it stands with France and Russia. Later today you are due to leave for a short weekend at your fishing cottage on the River Itchen in Hampshire, and Serbia’s deadline expires this evening.

voices.who: Buchanan (British ambassador in Russia, reporting what he told Sazonov)
voices.text: Direct British interests in Serbia were nil, and a war on behalf of that country would never be sanctioned by British public opinion.

voices.who: Crowe (Assistant Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, minute on the telegram)
voices.text: Should the war come, and England stand aside, one of two things must happen: — (a.) Either Germany and Austria win, crush France, and humiliate Russia. (…) what will be the position of a friendless England? (b.) Or France and Russia win. What would then be their attitude towards England?

choices.text: Have Buchanan tell Sazonov that British opinion will not allow a war for Serbia, so Russia should not hurry to mobilize
choices.why: Slowing Russia’s mobilization is the fastest way to head off a war
choices.after: Sazonov was furious that Britain seemed to be washing its hands of Europe. Paléologue reported to Paris that Britain could not be relied on, and the Russian General Staff went on preparing to mobilize whatever Britain said.

choices.text: As Crowe’s minute urges, press the Cabinet to decide and announce that the fleet will mobilize as soon as any Great Power does
choices.why: Germany will stop only if it believes Britain will fight
choices.after: You canceled the weekend’s fishing and stayed in London. Nicolson and Crowe were pleased, but Asquith asked you not to let a word out before Monday’s Cabinet. By Sunday morning ministers were whispering that the foreign secretary might resign.

choices.text: Make no declaration of solidarity; remain a friend who can talk to both sides, and ask Germany to join in mediation
choices.why: Only by staying a mediator can Britain bring Berlin to the table
choices.after: You made no declaration of solidarity. That afternoon, minutes before the deadline, Serbia delivered its reply, but the Austrian minister, Giesl, at once announced the breaking off of relations and left Belgrade by train. You set off for Hampshire as planned.

note.text: Permanent Under-Secretary Nicolson had been ambassador to Russia from 1906 to 1910 and had negotiated the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907. Crowe was born in Leipzig and had a German mother and a German wife, yet he was the Foreign Office’s leading anti-German voice and in 1907 wrote a famous memorandum warning of German expansion.

GB-03.place: Fishing cottage at Itchen Abbas, Hampshire
GB-03.title: A Telegram by the River

telegram.text: Draft proposal for London conference of ambassadors of Britain, Germany, France and Italy / Request to Vienna, Belgrade and St Petersburg to suspend military operations during conference / If approved please telegraph resident clerk

GB-03.event: On the afternoon of 25 July Serbia delivered its reply just before the deadline, and Austria and Serbia both began to mobilize that day.
GB-03.scene: You and your wife, Dorothy, who died in a carriage accident in 1906, loved this small cottage on the Itchen. With its clear, trout-filled river and its birdsong, it is the one place where you can escape the noise of the Foreign Office, but this Sunday London’s telegrams have reached even here. Permanent Under-Secretary Nicolson has sent a draft proposing a conference of ambassadors in London, as in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913, but this time with only the four powers that have no direct stake. Serbia, for its part, has replied, accepting most of Austria’s demands, yet Austria has broken off relations and begun a partial mobilization.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: If a conference can only be convened, we gain time. We must ask Austria, Serbia and Russia all to suspend military operations while it sits. In 1913, too, the ambassadors in London kept the peace.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, in his notes that day)
voices.text: Anyhow, it is the most dangerous situation of the last forty years.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: I will advise Berlin to accept a conference. But Berlin will be wary of a conference that seems to put its ally before a European tribunal, and it will prefer direct talks between Vienna and St Petersburg.

choices.text: Drop the conference plan and work behind the scenes for the direct talks between Vienna and St Petersburg that Berlin prefers
choices.why: Insisting on a form Berlin dislikes would cost Britain Germany’s cooperation
choices.after: Sazonov tried direct talks with Vienna, but Austria refused to treat Serbia’s reply as a basis for negotiation. Britain had, in effect, stepped back from its place as mediator.

choices.text: Approve Nicolson’s draft: hold a conference of four ambassadors in London and ask that military operations stop while it sits
choices.why: As in 1913, simply getting the ambassadors together will buy time
choices.after: At 2 p.m. you replied from Itchen Abbas approving Nicolson’s draft and telling him to send it. Italy and France soon accepted, but the next day Germany refused, saying the conference would amount to a court of arbitration sitting in judgment on its ally.

choices.text: Propose the conference and at the same time warn Lichnowsky in advance that if France is drawn in, Britain will not stand aside
choices.why: A conference carries weight only if a warning goes with it
choices.after: Lichnowsky telegraphed the warning to Berlin three days before such a warning was in fact given. For the first time Berlin had to reckon with British intervention, and Bethmann Hollweg began drafting a reply accepting a conference in another form.

note.text: The London Conference of Ambassadors, which Grey chaired from December 1912 to August 1913, dealt with the aftermath of the Balkan Wars, including Albanian independence, and kept the Great Powers out of war. That is why Grey turned first to the same method in July 1914.

pressure.title: The Cottage and Your Failing Eyes
pressure.text: You and your wife, Dorothy, who died in February 1906 after being thrown from a carriage, built the cottage at Itchen Abbas in 1890. Two months ago, in May, two eye specialists told you that you would not go completely blind but would lose the power to read. You have decided to go to Germany to consult a well-known oculist there once the parliamentary session is over.

GB-04.place: 33 Eccleston Square, London (the house Grey rented from Churchill)
GB-04.title: Disperse the Fleet?
GB-04.event: On the afternoon of 26 July British troops fired on a crowd at Bachelor’s Walk in Dublin, killing three and wounding more than thirty (one of the wounded died in September, bringing the dead to four). The same day the Irish Volunteers landed German rifles at Howth.
GB-04.scene: In mid-July, instead of its summer maneuvers, the navy held a test mobilization that called up even the reserves, ending with a grand review at Spithead attended by the King on 17 and 18 July. The First and Second Fleets were gathered at Portland and were due to disperse from 7 a.m. on Monday, 27 July. Churchill, the First Lord, had been with his family at Cromer on the Norfolk coast; after a telephone call at noon with the First Sea Lord, Prince Louis of Battenberg, he returned to the Admiralty at 9 p.m. In the meantime Prince Louis had ordered the fleet not to disperse. Late tonight, after your return from Itchen Abbas, Churchill calls at his own house, where you are his tenant, and asks whether it would help to make this public.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: The reservists have all gone home, but the fleet is still together. Whether holding it together will help or harm is for the foreign secretary to decide.

voices.who: Tyrrell (Grey’s private secretary, gist)
voices.text: It should be announced as soon as possible. It may bring the Central Powers to their senses and calm Europe.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: If we call ourselves mediators and then rattle the fleet, Berlin will take it as a threat. Britain must move carefully.

choices.text: Let the fleet disperse on the morning of 27 July as planned, so no one can say Britain took the first military step
choices.why: Whoever takes the first military step will be blamed for the crisis
choices.after: The fleet dispersed to its home ports, and Churchill warned that it would take days to gather it again. In Paris people said that Britain was taking the crisis lightly.

choices.text: Accept Morley’s concern: keep the fleet at Portland but issue no Admiralty notice, and let the matter rest quietly
choices.why: A mediator who flaunts his strength loses his credit as mediator
choices.after: The fleet stayed at Portland, and the newspapers were quiet. Even so, the German naval attaché in London reported to Berlin that the Royal Navy was quietly preparing to mobilize.

choices.text: Keep the fleet together and announce it at once, as a signal that Britain takes this crisis seriously
choices.why: Fleet movements will wake Berlin and Vienna sooner than words
choices.after: The next morning every newspaper carried an Admiralty notice that the First Fleet, concentrated at Portland, would not disperse for the present. You explained to the Austrian ambassador, Mensdorff, that there was no menace in this; it expressed anxiety about the possibility of a European war.

note.text: According to Churchill’s memoir, the Grand Fleet assembled at its northern war station on 1 August 1914 had 24 capital ships of Dreadnought class or better (battleships and battle cruisers), yet its margin over the German High Seas Fleet was only seven Dreadnoughts. Prince Louis of Battenberg, who held the fleet together that day, was forced out that October by anti-German feeling because of his German princely family.

GB-05.title: Do Not Be Misled by the Friendly Tone
GB-05.event: On 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, and on 29 July Russia announced a partial mobilization.
GB-05.scene: Austria declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and from the early hours of the 29th shells fell on Belgrade. Russia announced a partial mobilization of the four military districts nearest the Austrian frontier. The morning Cabinet decided to promise nothing to either France or Germany, and the Admiralty sent the fleet a warning telegram that day. In the afternoon you see first Cambon and then Lichnowsky. Lichnowsky is an ambassador who truly loves England, and all July he has been warning Berlin that Britain will in the end stand with France.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, letter to his wife the day before)
voices.text: Everything tends towards catastrophe and collapse. I am interested, geared up and happy. Is it not horrible to be built like that?

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: The Cabinet has decided to promise nothing to either side. A word from the foreign secretary must not take the place of a Cabinet decision.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Remember the letters of 1912. If peace were seriously threatened, the two governments would consult on what to do. Peace has never been more threatened than it is now.

choices.text: Warn Lichnowsky privately, while telling Cambon that Britain has promised nothing
choices.why: Neither Berlin nor Paris should be emboldened by counting on Britain
choices.after: You told Lichnowsky not to be misled by the friendly tone of your conversations into thinking that Britain would stand aside. He replied that this matched the view he had already reported to Berlin. The same day you appealed to Berlin that mediation could come into operation by any method Germany liked, if only Germany would "press the button" in the interests of peace.

choices.text: Warn Germany, and also have Buchanan tell Russia not to expect British support if it moves to general mobilization
choices.why: A mediator’s word carries weight only if both sides are held back alike
choices.after: Sazonov protested that Britain was turning its back at the decisive moment. Nicholas II hesitated, but the Russian General Staff kept pressing for general mobilization.

choices.text: In line with the Cabinet majority, hint that Britain will not enter a continental quarrel as long as Belgium is left untouched
choices.why: Apart from Belgium, nothing will move the Cabinet and Parliament
choices.after: Berlin was relieved when Lichnowsky’s telegram arrived. The German General Staff counted on British neutrality, and that night Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg prepared an offer meant to secure it.

note.text: That morning the First Fleet left Portland and that night ran at high speed, without lights, through the Strait of Dover toward its war base at Scapa Flow, north of Scotland. Churchill feared the move might look provocative, so he did not bring it before the Cabinet and obtained only the Prime Minister’s approval.

GB-06.title: Will You Sell France?

telegram.text: Chancellor asks for British neutrality / Even if victorious Germany will seek no territory in metropolitan France / Declines to give same assurance for French colonies / Belgium’s integrity respected after war if she does not side against Germany / Neutrality of Holland respected

GB-06.scene: At 9 a.m. Ambassador Goschen’s telegram arrives from Berlin. Late last night Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg called him in and proposed that if Britain stayed neutral, Germany, even if victorious, would take no territory from metropolitan France. He refused any promise about the French colonies, and on Belgium he said only that its territory would be preserved after the war if it did not side against Germany, which amounted to an admission that Germany would march through Belgium. The same morning the Bank of England raised its rate, and Asquith agrees with the Conservative leaders to postpone the Irish Amending Bill.

voices.who: Crowe (Assistant Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, minute on the telegram)
voices.text: The only comment that need be made on these astounding proposals is that they reflect discredit on the statesman who makes them.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, in his notes that day)
voices.text: The City, which is in a terrible state of depression and paralysis, is for the time being all against English intervention.

choices.text: Mindful of the non-interventionists, say Britain will weigh neutrality if Germany spares Belgium and France’s coast and colonies
choices.why: Raising the terms makes Germany pay the price of British neutrality
choices.after: Berlin could never bring itself to promise to leave Belgium alone, because the German army had no plan of operations except one that went through Belgium. Cambon was enraged to hear that Britain had made France a bargaining counter.

choices.text: Telegraph a refusal to Goschen: a bargain at the expense of France would be a disgrace to Britain’s good name
choices.why: Sell a friend once and no one will ever trust Britain again
choices.after: You telegraphed Goschen that it would be a disgrace to make this bargain with Germany at the expense of France, a disgrace from which the good name of this country would never recover. Yet you added that if this crisis passed, you would work for an arrangement assuring Germany that France, Russia and Britain would pursue no policy aimed against her.

choices.text: Accept if metropolitan France is safe; with the City paralyzed, there is no reason for Britain to enter a continental war
choices.why: If metropolitan France is safe, Britain’s own interests are safe too
choices.after: When they heard your decision, Nicolson and Crowe said they would put in their resignations. Berlin was relieved, and Paris was stunned.

note.text: Crowe, though born in Leipzig and of German descent, was the Foreign Office’s most determined anti-German official, and in his minute on this telegram he noted that Germany had all but admitted it intended to violate Belgian neutrality.

GB-07.title: The Precedent of 1870
GB-07.clock: Germany’s ultimatum to Russia (12 hours from delivery) is on its way to St Petersburg
GB-07.event: On the afternoon of 30 July Nicholas II approved general mobilization; on 31 July Germany proclaimed a "state of imminent danger of war" and demanded that Russia stop mobilizing within 12 hours.
GB-07.scene: Today the London Stock Exchange has closed, and bankers in the City are crying out that British entry into the war would wreck credit. The 11 a.m. Cabinet debated Belgian neutrality at length but promised nothing. This morning you went so far as to tell Lichnowsky that if Germany put forward a reasonable proposal and Russia and France rejected it, Britain would have nothing more to do with the consequences, though you added that if France were drawn in, Britain would be drawn in too. In the afternoon Cambon calls and asks once more whether Britain will help if Germany attacks France. In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, Gladstone’s government obtained a pledge from each belligerent to respect Belgian neutrality.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, in his notes that day)
voices.text: Of course everybody longs to stand aside.

voices.who: Crowe (Assistant Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, memorandum that day)
voices.text: The argument that there is no written bond binding us to France is strictly correct. There is no contractual obligation. But the Entente has been made, strengthened, put to the test and celebrated in a manner justifying the belief that a moral bond was being forged.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: In 1870 Britain made the great mistake of letting German power grow enormously. Britain is about to repeat that mistake.

choices.text: Citing the moral bond in Crowe’s memorandum, promise Cambon you will lead the Cabinet to fight alongside France if Germany attacks
choices.why: France cannot be expected to hold out alone without any promise
choices.after: Cambon telegraphed Paris that you had given your personal promise. Most of the Cabinet know nothing of it, and if they find out, the Cabinet may break apart.

choices.text: Leave the Belgian question unraised for now; demanding answers in advance would only harden Germany’s war plan
choices.why: A question that forces an answer only drives the other side into a corner
choices.after: The Belgian question was left unresolved. The Cabinet’s non-interventionists were relieved that one more reason for Britain to intervene had vanished.

choices.text: Ask France and Germany, as Gladstone’s government did in 1870, whether each will respect Belgian neutrality
choices.why: Putting the treaty first can bring the Cabinet and Parliament along
choices.after: France answered that night that it would. Germany’s state secretary for foreign affairs, Jagow, evaded the question, saying he must consult the Emperor and the Chancellor and that any answer would reveal part of the war plan. Belgium was becoming the key issue that could move the British Cabinet.

note.text: As stock exchanges across Europe closed in late July, sell orders poured into London. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4 percent on 30 July, 8 percent on the 31st and 10 percent on 1 August, and the London Stock Exchange closed on 31 July and stayed shut for nearly five months.

pressure.title: The City Shuts Its Doors
pressure.text: On 31 July the London Stock Exchange closed, and the Bank of England raised its rate to 8 percent that day. The day before, Asquith had written that the City, "in a terrible state of depression and paralysis," was "for the time being all against English intervention." The City’s financiers are pleading with the government that British entry into the war would wreck credit, and Chancellor Lloyd George is absorbed in measures to head off a financial panic. The more you speak of intervention, the more the anger of the Liberals and the City falls on you.

GB-08.title: A Misunderstanding on the Telephone

telegram.text: State Secretary Jagow evades immediate answer on respect for Belgian neutrality / Must consult Emperor and Chancellor / Fears any reply would disclose part of plan of campaign

GB-08.event: At 5 p.m. on 1 August Germany ordered general mobilization, and that evening it declared war on Russia.
GB-08.scene: At about 1:30 a.m. Asquith took a taxi to Buckingham Palace, where the King, roused from bed and in his dressing gown, approved a last telegram of appeal to Nicholas II. At 11 a.m. the Cabinet meets again, and you have made up your mind to resign if it chooses non-intervention at any price. Earlier this morning your secretary, Tyrrell, called on Lichnowsky, and now you telephone the ambassador yourself with a thought: if Germany does not attack France in the west, perhaps at least half of a continental war could be prevented. German general mobilization is now only a matter of time.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, in his notes that day)
voices.text: Grey declares that if an out-and-out and uncompromising policy of non-intervention at all costs is adopted he will go. Winston very bellicose and demanding immediate mobilization.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: If Germany promises not to attack France, can Britain guarantee French neutrality? I need something to persuade Berlin.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: The moment we ask France to abandon Russia, the entente is finished. France will never accept neutrality on those terms.

choices.text: Promise nothing on Lichnowsky’s terms and simply demand again the clear answer on Belgium that Jagow evaded
choices.why: Keeping Britain’s hands free is the strongest move on the board
choices.after: Lichnowsky asked whether Britain would stay neutral if Germany respected Belgium, but you answered that you could not promise on that condition alone and that Britain’s hands were still free. He went on to offer the integrity of France and her colonies, but you declined.
choices.realNote: Grey did give this answer that afternoon. But the misunderstanding created by the morning telephone conversation was not avoided.

choices.text: Sound out Lichnowsky by telephone: if Germany does not attack France, is there no way for France to remain neutral?
choices.why: If even half of a continental war can be prevented, the attempt is worth making
choices.after: Lichnowsky took this to mean that Britain would guarantee French neutrality and telegraphed Berlin, and Wilhelm II briefly halted the advance in the west. But that night King George V’s reply said there had been a misunderstanding, and the German army moved again. In the afternoon you told Cambon that France must take her own decision without counting on help that Britain was not now in a position to promise. Cambon said he could not transmit that answer to Paris.

choices.text: Turn the idea discussed with Lichnowsky into a formal note: Britain stays neutral if Germany attacks neither France nor Belgium
choices.why: If the west stays quiet, Britain can stay out of the war
choices.after: After Lichnowsky’s telegram, a formal British note arrived in Berlin. Wilhelm II overrode Moltke’s objections and halted the deployment in the west, and Cambon was furious that Britain was asking France to abandon Russia.

note.text: The misunderstanding began with the telegram Lichnowsky sent at 11:14 that morning. Historians disagree about whether Grey’s telephone call was simple confusion or a genuine attempt to sound Germany out before the Cabinet decided. When Lichnowsky’s 1916 memorandum, My Mission to London, was published abroad in the spring of 1918, he lost his seat in the Prussian House of Lords that July.

GB-09.title: The Channel Pledge

telegram.from: Buckingham Palace (King George V to Wilhelm II)
telegram.text: There must be some misunderstanding as to a suggestion that passed in friendly conversation between Prince Lichnowsky and Sir Edward Grey this afternoon

GB-09.scene: Lichnowsky came to Asquith at breakfast and, in tears, begged him not to let Britain side with France. During the night Churchill, with the Prime Minister’s tacit consent, ordered the fleet mobilized, and this morning German troops entered Luxembourg. Since the 1912 agreement on fleet dispositions France has kept the main body of its battleships in the Mediterranean, so the Channel and the northern coast of France are virtually unguarded. The Cabinet, which began at 11 a.m., runs on until nearly 2 p.m., and it grows plain that the government may split.

voices.who: Bonar Law and Lansdowne (Conservative leaders, letter to Asquith)
voices.text: It would be fatal to the honour and security of the United Kingdom to hesitate in supporting France and Russia at the present juncture.

voices.who: Burns (President of the Board of Trade, gist)
voices.text: A promise to defend the Channel is as good as a declaration of war. I cannot put my name to such a decision.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, in his notes that day)
voices.text: We have no obligation of any kind either to France or Russia to give them military or naval help. (…) We cannot allow Germany to use the Channel as a hostile base. We have obligations to Belgium to prevent it being utilized and absorbed by Germany.

choices.text: Citing the 1912 fleet agreement, ask the Cabinet to pledge that the fleet will stop any German attack on France’s Channel coast
choices.why: A coast left bare under the 1912 agreement is Britain’s to defend
choices.after: The Cabinet agreed with difficulty, and in the afternoon you handed Cambon a memorandum: the British fleet would give all the protection in its power, subject to the support of Parliament. Burns announced his resignation on the spot, and Morley followed. The evening Cabinet decided that a substantial violation of Belgian neutrality would compel British action, and at that hour in Brussels the German minister was delivering an ultimatum demanding passage for German troops.

choices.text: As Burns and Morley wish, refuse the coastal pledge: Britain will not enter this war unless it is directly attacked
choices.why: A Channel pledge would be more than the Cabinet and the party can bear
choices.after: Cambon reminded you once more that France had left its northern coast bare because of the 1912 fleet agreement, and left without another word. The Conservatives signaled a motion of no confidence, and Crowe and Nicolson began drafting their resignations.

choices.text: Backed by the Conservative leaders' letter, stake your resignation on sending all six expeditionary divisions to France at once
choices.why: Half a promise cannot save France in the first battle
choices.after: After Morley and Burns, Simon and Beauchamp also resigned, and Lloyd George kept silent to the end. To save the government, Asquith even weighed a coalition with the Conservatives. France was moved, but Liberal backbenchers protested that the foreign secretary had run ahead of Parliament.

note.text: In his notes that day Asquith set out six principles, including that "it is against British interests that France should be wiped out as a Great Power," and he stated firmly that sending the Expeditionary Force to France at this moment was "out of the question." The Channel pledge was not a promise to go to war; it was a decision that bought time to see how the Belgian question would turn out.

map.caption: On the morning of 2 August German troops entered Luxembourg by way of Troisvierges; since the 1912 agreement, the defense of France’s northern coast had relied on the British fleet.

GB-10.title: Let Every Man Look into His Own Heart

telegram.from: Brussels (King Albert I of the Belgians to George V)
telegram.text: I make a supreme appeal to the diplomatic intervention of Your Majesty’s Government to safeguard the integrity of Belgium

GB-10.event: At 7 p.m. on 2 August Germany sent Belgium a 12-hour demand for passage for its troops, and on the morning of 3 August the Belgian government refused. That evening Germany declared war on France.
GB-10.scene: It is Bank Holiday Monday, and crowds waiting for news fill Whitehall and Parliament Square. Last night Germany demanded passage through Belgium for its army, and this morning the Belgian government refused. At the morning Cabinet Asquith reported the resignations of Morley, Burns, Simon and Beauchamp, and he hopes that at least some of them will reconsider (Simon and Beauchamp will in the end stay; Morley and Burns will go). The German embassy has let it be known that Germany will not attack France’s northern coast if Britain stays neutral. You have had only a few hours to work on your speech, and every seat in the chamber is taken.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: Now that Belgium has chosen to fight, the Liberal Party will follow. Faced with a small nation’s treaty being trampled, even the peace men have nothing left to say.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, now resigned, gist)
voices.text: Belgium is only a pretext. This war will put Britain on the side of Russian autocracy and destroy everything the Liberal Party has stood for.

choices.text: Lay it all out, the 1912 letters, the Channel pledge and the Belgian treaty, and leave the judgment to each member’s conscience
choices.why: A promise kept hidden will in the end divide Parliament and the country
choices.after: When your speech of an hour or so ended, the House was overwhelmingly with you. Bonar Law for the Conservatives and Redmond for the Irish Nationalists declared their support, while Ramsay MacDonald of the Labour Party countered that the government was wrong. As you left the chamber, Churchill asked what would happen now, and you answered that Germany would be sent an ultimatum to stop the invasion of Belgium within 24 hours.

choices.text: So that Liberal backbenchers can accept it, stress only the duties of the 1839 treaty and say nothing about relations with France
choices.why: Only a small nation’s treaty can unite the Liberal Party
choices.after: Liberal members were relieved, but Cambon was aghast at a speech that left out the Channel pledge. The Conservatives attacked the government for hiding its relations with France.

choices.text: Promise to return to Parliament once German troops are confirmed across the Belgian frontier, and defer a decision today
choices.why: Only an invasion no one can deny will bring the opponents along
choices.after: The House stirred uneasily, and the Conservatives denounced the government for hesitating. The next morning came word that German troops had crossed the Belgian frontier.

note.text: In his speech Grey said that, as to how far friendship with France entailed obligation, "let every man look into his own heart, and his own feelings, and construe the extent of the obligation for himself," and that "the one bright spot in the whole of this terrible situation is Ireland." Ramsay MacDonald replied: "I think he is wrong. (…) I think the verdict of history will be that they are wrong."

GB-11.title: Until Midnight
GB-11.clock: Deadline 11 p.m. London time (midnight in Berlin)

telegram.text: Military attaché informed at War Office that German troops have entered Belgian territory / Liège summoned to surrender by small party of Germans, who were repulsed

GB-11.event: On the morning of 4 August German troops crossed the Belgian frontier.
GB-11.scene: Berlin has not answered the first telegram you sent this morning, which asked for an assurance that Belgian neutrality would be respected. By now German troops have crossed Belgium’s eastern frontier and are heading for the fortress of Liège. In the Mediterranean the battle cruisers Indomitable and Indefatigable have caught up with the German battle cruiser Goeben. Churchill asked for leave to engage at once if the Goeben attacked French troop transports, and the Prime Minister and you agreed, but the Cabinet decided that no act of war should be committed before the deadline. Field Marshal Kitchener, about to return to Egypt, was recalled to London from Dover yesterday. The text of the final telegram lies before you.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: We have the Goeben in sight. Let us engage at once if she attacks the French transports. It would be a great misfortune to lose her in the night.

voices.who: The Cabinet majority (gist of that day’s decision)
voices.text: No act of war may be committed until the ultimatum has expired. We cannot let Britain’s good faith be impugned for the sake of sinking one ship.

choices.text: Put off war: send no army, let the fleet guard the Channel and the Belgian coast, and fund and arm Belgium
choices.why: Holding the sea alone is enough to keep Britain safe
choices.after: German troops passed Liège and advanced on Brussels, and France had to accept that no British expeditionary force was coming. The Conservatives and the newspapers raged that Britain had abandoned a treaty.

choices.text: Send Berlin an ultimatum: unless the violation of Belgium stops by midnight Berlin time, it means war
choices.why: If Britain does not honor this treaty, no promise of hers will be believed
choices.after: No German answer came. That evening Bethmann Hollweg raged at Goschen, who had come to take his leave, that "just for a scrap of paper" Britain was going to make war on a kindred nation. At 11 p.m. London time, as Big Ben struck, the Admiralty telegraphed every British ship in the world to commence hostilities against Germany.

note.text: The British Expeditionary Force, created by War Secretary Haldane’s reforms of 1906–1908, consisted of six infantry divisions and one cavalry division, small beside the multimillion-man armies of the continent. Asquith, who had also been serving as war secretary since the Curragh incident in March 1914, made Kitchener secretary of state for war on 5 August, and the expeditionary force crossed first with four infantry divisions and one cavalry division.

map.caption: On the morning of 4 August German troops crossed Belgium’s eastern frontier and headed for the fortress of Liège.

GB-12.title: Where to Send the Army
GB-12.event: At 11 p.m. on 4 August (London time) Britain went to war with Germany.
GB-12.scene: This afternoon, the day after the declaration of war, Asquith has called an unprecedented war council at Downing Street. Around one table sit you and the other ministers who had led the country into war, the heads of the army and navy, Field Marshal Sir John French, chosen to command the expeditionary force, the corps commander Douglas Haig, Kitchener, soon to be war secretary, and Field Marshal Roberts, 81. French had resigned as Chief of the Imperial General Staff over the Curragh incident in March, and now he is to lead the army going to the continent. The council must decide whether to send all six divisions or keep some at home, and where to concentrate them.

voices.who: Sir John French (commander of the Expeditionary Force, gist)
voices.text: We can cross at once and settle the destination later. There is also the option of making Antwerp our base and fighting alongside the Belgian army.

voices.who: Kitchener (soon to be war secretary, gist)
voices.text: The expeditionary force should concentrate around Amiens, and first we must be in close touch with the French army. This war will not be short, so we must raise new armies numbering in the millions.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: The navy’s mobilization is complete and the Strait of Dover is closed tight. The fleet will guard the island, so for the navy’s part all six divisions may go at once.

choices.text: Trust Churchill’s word that the fleet will guard the island, and send all six divisions to France at once
choices.why: The troops available for the first battle must not be held back
choices.after: Some generals worried that the home country would be left bare, but the Cabinet sided with Churchill and Haldane. Six divisions gathered before Mons, and home defense was left to the still half-trained Territorial Force.

choices.text: Take Sir John French’s suggestion and send the force to Antwerp to strike the flank of the German right wing with the Belgians
choices.why: Better to seek a decisive blow of Britain’s own than follow behind the French
choices.after: The navy objected that it could not protect the supply line of so large an army across the water, and the War Office had no plan at all for going to Antwerp. While the expeditionary force prepared a route no one had planned for, the far left of the French line stood empty.

choices.text: Heed those who fear a German landing: send four infantry divisions and one cavalry division first, and keep two at home
choices.why: Britain can defend the island and keep its promise on the continent
choices.after: On 6 August the Cabinet decided to send four infantry divisions and one cavalry division first, and the expeditionary force was to concentrate near Maubeuge, at the far left of the French line. The force crossed the Channel between 9 and 22 August, and you later recalled that the four divisions reached France in less time than planned.

note.text: During the Curragh incident of March 1914, Henry Wilson, Director of Military Operations, was said to have encouraged the officers' threat to resign from behind the scenes, and the affair forced out Chief of the Imperial General Staff French and War Secretary Seely. Five months later French and Wilson crossed to the continent as commander and sub-chief of staff of the expeditionary force.

map.caption: The expeditionary force gathered near Maubeuge on the French frontier, southwest of Namur; some had proposed sending it to Antwerp.

GB-13.title: Japan, the Ally

telegram.text: Foreign Minister Kato strongly opposes withdrawal of British request / Japanese Cabinet decided on 8th to send ultimatum to Germany, and Emperor has given sanction

GB-13.event: On 7 August you asked Japan to hunt down and destroy German armed merchant cruisers.
GB-13.scene: On 7 August, under the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, you asked Japan for its fleet to find and destroy the German armed merchant cruisers preying on British shipping. But Japan means to use this as the occasion for full-scale war with Germany and an attack on the German leasehold at Tsingtao. Australia and New Zealand fear that Japan will seize Germany’s Pacific islands, and American opinion is also wary of Japanese expansion. On the 10th you tried to withdraw the request, but Foreign Minister Kato protested strongly that a decision already made could not be reversed.

voices.who: Grey (you, in your later memoir)
voices.text: To explain to an Ally that her help will be welcome, but that you hope it will not be made inconvenient, is a proceeding that is neither agreeable nor gracious.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: The German East Asia Squadron and its armed merchantmen threaten the sea lanes of the Pacific and Indian Oceans. Without the Japanese fleet we cannot guard all those waters.

voices.who: Harcourt (Colonial Secretary, gist)
voices.text: Australia and New Zealand fear Japan moving into the South Pacific in Germany’s place. We must not lose the goodwill of the Dominions.

choices.text: Yield to Kato and accept Japan’s entry into the war, but propose limiting operations to Chinese waters and the German leasehold
choices.why: Take the ally’s help, but calm the fears of the Dominions and America too
choices.after: On 15 August Japan sent Germany an ultimatum to hand over the Tsingtao leasehold, and on 23 August it declared war. Britain told the press that Japanese operations would not extend beyond Chinese waters into the Pacific, but this announcement, made without telling Japan first, left resentment in Tokyo.

choices.text: Heed the Dominion fears Harcourt reports: withdraw the request for good and let the Royal Navy hunt the German cruisers itself
choices.why: Japan in the Pacific would leave Britain a heavier burden after the war
choices.after: Kato protested that an alliance could not be run to suit only one partner, and voices in Japan saying Britain could not be trusted grew louder. The German East Asia Squadron used the gap to slip across the Pacific toward South America.

choices.text: As the Admiralty wishes, accept without limits and leave Germany’s Pacific islands and the cruiser hunt to the Japanese navy
choices.why: Guarding vast oceans means using the ally’s fleet without stint
choices.after: The governments of Australia and New Zealand protested fiercely to London, and American newspapers accused Britain of handing the Pacific to Japan. In October the Japanese navy occupied Germany’s islands north of the equator.

note.text: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance, concluded in 1902, was renewed twice, in 1905 and 1911, and it allowed Britain to concentrate its main fleet in European waters. Japanese forces took Tsingtao in November 1914.

GB-14.title: The Greek Offer

telegram.text: Prime Minister Venizelos, with King’s approval, places all Greek naval and military resources at disposal of Entente / Britain in particular / 250,000 men can be mobilized

GB-14.event: On the evening of 10 August the German battle cruiser Goeben and the light cruiser Breslau entered the Dardanelles, and the Ottoman government announced that it had bought both ships.
GB-14.scene: The Goeben and the Breslau now fly the Ottoman flag, but their German crews have not left the ships, and two British battle cruisers are watching the two vessels outside the Straits. On 31 July Churchill posted guards on the Ottoman battleships nearing completion in British yards to keep the Ottoman sailors from boarding, and Britain took the two ships, the Sultan Osman I and the Reshadieh, into the Royal Navy. In the Ottoman Empire, where part of the price was raised by public subscription, anger at Britain runs high. Kitchener insists that war with the Ottomans must be avoided somehow until the Indian troops have passed through the Suez Canal, and Churchill is drawn to the Greek offer.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, minute to Grey, 12 August)
voices.text: In all the circumstances, the Admiralty agree that the sale or transfer of these two vessels to the Turkish flag should be allowed, provided that the transference is bona fide and permanent. The essential condition to insist on is that all the German officers and men of the crews of both ships must, without exception, be at once repatriated to Germany under parole not to serve again during the war.

voices.who: Kitchener (Secretary of State for War, gist)
voices.text: We must not fight the Ottomans until the Indian troops have passed safely through the Suez Canal on their way to France. Until then, give them no pretext of any kind.

voices.who: Mallet (British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, gist)
voices.text: The Grand Vizier and the neutral party are still holding out. Apart from Enver Pasha, most of the Ottoman leaders do not want war. We must buy time.

choices.text: As Churchill wishes, accept Venizelos’s offer and prepare to open the Dardanelles with the Greek army and navy
choices.why: If the Ottomans are to be enemies anyway, Britain should seize the Straits first
choices.after: The Greek General Staff brought out its long-prepared plan to occupy the peninsula on the north side of the Straits, and the Ottomans took Greek mobilization as preparation for war. From St Petersburg Sazonov sent London a pointed question: was Greece aiming at Constantinople?

choices.text: Trust Mallet’s reports: decline the Greek offer and, with France and Russia, promise to respect Ottoman territorial integrity
choices.why: Giving the Ottoman neutralists time will keep new fronts from opening
choices.after: The Cabinet followed you and declined Venizelos’s offer. Together with France and Russia you promised that if the Ottomans stayed neutral, their territory and independence would be guaranteed at the peace, but the German crews never left. At the end of October the Ottoman fleet, led by the Goeben, attacked Russian ports on the Black Sea, and the Ottoman Empire entered the war on Germany’s side.

choices.text: On Churchill’s 12 August terms, send the Ottomans an ultimatum: if the German crews do not leave, Britain will strike the Goeben
choices.why: The Goeben in German hands makes Ottoman neutrality a sham
choices.after: The Ottoman government took the ultimatum as an insult, and Enver Pasha used it as a pretext to hasten the alliance with Germany. The Ottoman Empire entered the war about two months earlier than it did in fact, and the troops coming from India faced an Ottoman threat at the Suez Canal.

note.text: The Sultan Osman I was a battleship originally ordered from Britain by Brazil; the Ottoman Empire bought it for £2.75 million in December 1913. On entering the Royal Navy it was renamed Agincourt, and the Reshadieh became Erin.

map.caption: The Goeben entered the Dardanelles on 10 August and made for Constantinople; Greece, Bulgaria and Romania were still neutral.

pressure.title: Diplomacy, the Handmaid of War
pressure.text: Once the war began, the Foreign Office’s work became serving the needs of the War Office and the Admiralty. As you later put it, "In war, however, diplomacy is the handmaid of the necessities of the War Office and the Admiralty." Kitchener demands that war with the Ottomans be avoided until the Indian troops have passed through the Suez Canal, and the Admiralty insists that the two Ottoman battleships cannot be handed back. You are left both to keep the Ottoman Empire neutral and to live with the anger a British decision has roused there.

GB-15G.title: A Plan for the Peninsula
GB-15G.scene: A little over ten days have passed since Britain decided to join hands with Greece. The army staff has calculated that seizing the peninsula on the north side of the Dardanelles would take 60,000 men, with 30,000 landing first and holding on for a week. The Greek army says it can provide more than that, but the Ottomans, watching Greece mobilize, have handed the defense of the Straits to German officers, and Bulgaria is looking for a chance to win back the land it lost in 1913. Above all, Russia does not want Greek troops to enter Constantinople first.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, telegram of 4 September to Admiral Kerr in Greece)
voices.text: In order that the right and obvious method of attack upon Turkey (viz. by striking immediately at the heart) may be carried out (…)

voices.who: Buchanan (British ambassador in Russia, gist)
voices.text: Sazonov will regard Greek troops in Constantinople as a betrayal of Russia. We must not move without Russia’s consent.

choices.text: Relying on Noel Buxton’s Balkan mission, put off the landing until Russia consents and Bulgaria joins in
choices.why: The battle for the Straits can be won only if the Balkan states stand together
choices.after: Bulgaria said it would not move unless Macedonia was returned, and Serbia and Greece refused to give up land. While the talks dragged on, the Ottoman fleet attacked Russia in the Black Sea at the end of October.

choices.text: Assure Sazonov that no one will reach for Constantinople, and back the Greek landing on the peninsula as the staff has planned
choices.why: Clear up Russia’s suspicions and the Straits can be opened quickly
choices.after: In late September the Greek army landed on the peninsula under cover of the British fleet, and the Ottoman Empire declared war on Germany’s side. The battle for the Straits began half a year before the actual campaign of 1915, under a different flag.

note.text: In 1914 Grey in fact persuaded the Cabinet to decline Venizelos’s offer, arguing that an alliance with Greece would at once bring war with the Ottomans, and perhaps with Bulgaria, and would arouse Russian suspicion.

GB-03D.title: A Warning Staked on Resignation
GB-03D.scene: Having stayed in London all weekend, you demand at Monday’s Cabinet that Britain’s position be stated in the Commons that very afternoon. Yesterday the navy decided not to disperse the fleet, and Germany is about to refuse the four-power conference. Across the table Morley and Burns sit stony-faced, while Lloyd George, gauging the mood of the Liberal backbenches, says little. By Churchill’s later account, three-quarters of the Cabinet are determined not to be drawn into a European quarrel unless Britain itself is attacked.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: Britain is to throw itself into a continental war because of Serbia? If such a declaration is made, I cannot remain in this Cabinet.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: The foreign secretary is right. Germany is bold only so long as it believes Britain will stand aside. The fleet is ready.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: Most Liberal members are against war. If we declare today, the Cabinet may survive, but the party may split.

choices.text: Give up the public declaration and instead warn Lichnowsky privately and plainly, on terms even Lloyd George can accept
choices.why: Britain can keep the Cabinet together and still send Berlin a signal
choices.after: The Cabinet agreed to a private warning. On receiving Lichnowsky’s telegram, Berlin began for the first time to reckon seriously with the possibility of British intervention, and Bethmann Hollweg replied that he could accept a conference in a different form.

choices.text: If Morley and Burns go, the government falls: withdraw the declaration and return to mediation to save the four-power conference
choices.why: A fallen government can neither mediate nor warn
choices.after: Nicolson was disappointed, and Cambon reported to Paris that Britain was putting off its decision. That day Germany refused the four-power conference, and you had to look for another path to mediation.

choices.text: Stake your resignation on being allowed to tell the Commons this afternoon that Britain will not stand aside if France is attacked
choices.why: Only a public pledge that Berlin cannot doubt will stop the war
choices.after: Asquith knew that losing you would bring down the government. Morley and Burns resigned, but the Cabinet held, and that afternoon you told the Commons that Britain would not stand by if France were attacked.

note.text: In the general election of December 1910 the Liberals won 272 seats, almost level with the Conservatives and Unionists (271), and they governed with the support of the Irish Nationalists and Labour. A foreign secretary who defied the majority of the Cabinet and the party could bring down the government itself.

GB-04D.title: Berlin Recalculates
GB-04D.event: On the morning of 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
GB-04D.scene: The British foreign secretary’s statement in the Commons was telegraphed overnight to every capital in Europe. Wilhelm II, back yesterday from his Norwegian cruise, is furious; Moltke says six British divisions are of no account, but Tirpitz at the navy fears for the fate of his fleet. Even so, Vienna declared war on Serbia this morning. At this moment, with Berlin wavering for the first time, the next move is yours.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: When Germany wavers, we must show it a way out. Give Austria a place to stop without losing face.

voices.who: Crowe (Assistant Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: The moment we ease the pressure, Berlin will think Britain was bluffing. The fleet must go to its war station.

choices.text: As Crowe advises, send the fleet to its northern war station and publicize the army’s preparations to keep up the pressure
choices.why: Ease the pressure and Berlin will decide that Britain was bluffing
choices.after: News that the First Fleet had sailed north put the German navy on edge. But Vienna began to suspect that Germany was wavering before Britain, and the Austrian military hurried to create a fait accompli.

choices.text: As Nicolson advises, propose that if Austria stops at Belgrade, the four powers will guarantee that Serbia keeps its promises
choices.why: Give Vienna room to step back and it can stop with its honor intact
choices.after: Passing the proposal to Vienna, Berlin said plainly for the first time that if Austria did not follow it, Germany could not answer for the consequences. Berchtold played for time and put off his reply.

note.text: Whether an earlier and clearer British commitment to France would have prevented the war is an old debate. Some argue that the German leadership was banking on British neutrality; others counter that a British pledge would have made Russia bolder.

GB-05D.title: St Petersburg Grows Bold
GB-05D.event: On 29 July Russia announced a partial mobilization of four military districts.
GB-05D.scene: A telegram from Ambassador Buchanan has arrived. Having heard Britain’s declaration, the Russian General Staff is pressing the Tsar to hurry general mobilization, saying there is no longer any reason to hesitate. Sazonov believes that with Britain on board, Germany too will back down. Britain’s declaration of solidarity may stop Berlin, but it may also set Russia moving without restraint.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: The moment we doubt Russia, the whole entente collapses. Put conditions on our support and the declaration loses its force.

voices.who: Buchanan (British ambassador in Russia, gist)
voices.text: Russian general mobilization is as good as a declaration of war on Germany. If Britain does not hold Russia back now, no one will.

choices.text: Have Buchanan tell Sazonov that British support holds only on the understanding that Russia does not move to general mobilization
choices.why: Only conditions on support can keep Russia’s mobilization in check
choices.after: Sazonov was angry, but Nicholas II ordered a halt at partial mobilization. Discontent grew on the Russian General Staff, but time had been gained.

choices.text: As Nicolson says, set Russia no conditions: a declaration of solidarity with conditions attached becomes empty words
choices.why: The moment an ally is doubted, the whole entente falls apart
choices.after: Sure of British support, the Russian General Staff pushed through general mobilization on 30 July. In Berlin Moltke says there is no reason to wait any longer.

note.text: Russian general mobilization meant moving the armies facing Germany as well, and Germany’s war plan, which aimed to strike France in the west before Russia finished mobilizing, treated it as the signal for war.

GB-06D.title: Vienna’s Answer
GB-06D.scene: Under pressure from Berlin, Vienna has sent its answer. The Austrian army will halt after occupying Belgrade and accept Great Power mediation, on condition that Russia too stops mobilizing. Conrad, the chief of the General Staff, is furious at missing the chance to finish Serbia. If a conference is to meet in London, you must decide what goes on its agenda.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: Vienna will come to a conference only if the occupation of Belgrade is accepted. As long as Serbia’s sovereignty is guaranteed, Russia can accept it too.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: A conference that accepts the occupation is a humiliation for Russia. If Russia gives way, the entente is finished.

choices.text: As Cambon wishes, make Austria’s withdrawal from Belgrade a precondition of the conference; Russia cannot be humiliated again
choices.why: If Russia gives way once more, the entente is finished
choices.after: Vienna protested but, under pressure from Berlin, agreed at least to attend. Conrad kept preparing to advance, waiting for the conference to fail.

choices.text: Convene the London conference at once, accepting Belgrade’s occupation as a pledge but guaranteeing Serbia’s sovereignty and land
choices.why: Accept the occupation and Vienna will sit down at the table
choices.after: Vienna and Berlin replied that they would send delegates. But in the countries that had begun to mobilize, troop movements running on railway timetables moved faster than the conference.

GB-07DW.title: When Deterrence Fails
GB-07DW.event: On 30 July Russia began general mobilization, and on 31 July Germany sent Russia an ultimatum.
GB-07DW.scene: Russia began general mobilization on 30 July, and on 31 July Germany proclaimed a "state of imminent danger of war" and sent Russia a 12-hour ultimatum. Britain’s declaration of solidarity did not stop Berlin. Cambon comes to the Foreign Office every day asking Britain to keep its word, and the City has closed the Stock Exchange. Britain must now decide whether to act as it declared.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Britain has spoken before the world. If it draws back now, no one will believe Britain’s word again.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: We made the declaration, but Parliament has not yet agreed to war. We must look for a way out to the very end.

choices.text: Stand by the declaration: mobilize the fleet and tell Berlin Britain will fight at once if Germany attacks France or Belgium
choices.why: Fail to act as promised and Britain’s word will never carry weight again
choices.after: Berlin received the notice but did not change its war plan. Germany’s only plan was to strike France first by way of Belgium.

choices.text: Look for a last way out, as Lloyd George says: offer to hold France back if Germany does not attack in the west
choices.why: A war Parliament has not agreed to must be avoided to the last
choices.after: Cambon stormed out of the Foreign Office, calling it betrayal. Berlin wavered briefly, but Moltke flatly said the deployment in the west could not be changed.

GB-08DW.title: The Promised War
GB-08DW.event: On the morning of 4 August German troops crossed the Belgian frontier.
GB-08DW.scene: German troops crossed the Belgian frontier on the morning of 4 August. This time Parliament did not hesitate, and apart from a few who left the Cabinet, the government held together. What remains is the expeditionary force: Henry Wilson of the General Staff insists that all six divisions must go at once to the far left of the French line, while some ministers and generals want two divisions kept back against a German landing.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: So long as the navy holds the Channel, a German landing is impossible. Send the whole expeditionary force.

voices.who: Asquith (Prime Minister, gist)
voices.text: With home defense and Ireland to think of, we cannot send them all out at once.

choices.text: Accept Asquith’s concern: send four divisions first and keep the other two for home defense and Ireland
choices.why: Easing fears at home is what lets Britain endure a long war
choices.after: Four divisions crossed first, and the rest followed a few weeks later. France was disappointed that the British force was so small, but Britain went to war united from the start.
choices.realNote: This is close to what happened: the first contingent was four infantry divisions and one cavalry division, and the remaining divisions followed.

choices.text: On Henry Wilson’s plan, send all six divisions at once to the far left of the French line to guard its flank in the first battle
choices.why: The first battle will decide the outcome of the whole war
choices.after: The whole expeditionary force arrived before Mons. But the German right wing was far larger, and the war began to run longer than anyone had calculated.

note.text: In fact, the war councils of 5 and 6 August decided to send the expeditionary force initially as four infantry divisions and one cavalry division, which first met the Germans at Mons on 23 August.

GB-05C.title: Berlin Comes to the Table
GB-05C.event: On the morning of 28 July Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.
GB-05C.scene: Your early warning to Lichnowsky has changed Berlin’s calculations. Bethmann Hollweg replied that Germany would send an ambassador to a London conference, provided it did not take the form of a "court of arbitration." But Vienna declared war on Serbia this morning, and Belgrade, across the Sava and the Danube, lies within range of Austrian gunboats. It will still take nearly two weeks for the Austrian army to be ready to advance in earnest.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Berlin has agreed to the conference. But if it is a conference where Austria gains nothing, Vienna will leave the table.

voices.who: Crowe (Assistant Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: One cannot negotiate while making war. First the guns must fall silent.

choices.text: As Crowe says, demand an immediate ceasefire from Austria and Serbia before the conference; no one can negotiate under gunfire
choices.why: Talks held while fighting only buy time for the stronger side
choices.after: Vienna took the ceasefire demand as an insult, and Berlin, busy soothing Vienna, postponed the date of the conference. Meanwhile, in the early hours of 29 July, the first shells fell on Belgrade.

choices.text: Accept Austria’s occupation of Belgrade as a pledge for the conference, and see that its army goes no farther
choices.why: Vienna must be given something in hand, or the conference will break up
choices.after: Your proposal matched the "halt in Belgrade" idea that occurred to Wilhelm II that same day. This time Berlin passed it to Vienna as a clear demand.

note.text: Austria hurried to declare war on 28 July, but the earliest date on which Conrad’s army could advance into Serbia in earnest was around 12 August. Those two weeks were the time left to diplomacy.

GB-06C.title: Russia’s Clock
GB-06C.event: On 29 July Russia announced a partial mobilization, and President Poincaré returned to France.
GB-06C.scene: Russia announced a partial mobilization of four military districts on 29 July, and the chief of staff, Yanushkevich, is pressing the Tsar to switch to general mobilization, saying partial mobilization is technically impossible. President Poincaré landed at Dunkirk on 29 July. Mobilization may outrun diplomacy before the conference even meets.

voices.who: Buchanan (British ambassador in Russia, gist)
voices.text: Sazonov has no faith in the conference. The only thing he trusts is a promise that Britain will in the end stand with Russia.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: To hold Russia back we must move Paris. St Petersburg listens to Paris more than to London.

choices.text: Leave Russia’s partial mobilization in place as pressure on Vienna, and do not discourage it until Austria backs down
choices.why: Vienna will give ground at the conference only when Russian strength is visible
