choices.after: Russia moved to general mobilization, and the German General Staff now says it cannot wait a single day. The conference met, but mobilization running on railway timetables moved faster than the talks.

choices.text: Promise Sazonov that if Russia stops at partial mobilization, the conference will secure Serbia’s sovereignty and territory
choices.why: Russia will stop mobilizing only if it sees a sure reward
choices.after: Trusting the British promise, Nicholas II held back the order for general mobilization. The Russian General Staff fretted at falling behind day by day.

choices.text: As Nicolson advises, work through Paris and have the Viviani government urge Russia to hold back its mobilization
choices.why: St Petersburg listens to Paris more than to London
choices.after: Prime Minister Viviani urged Russia not to give Germany a pretext. Hearing this from its ally, Russia reluctantly slowed down.

note.text: Russia had no separate plan for a partial mobilization aimed only at Austria, and the General Staff argued that partial mobilization would actually throw general mobilization into disorder.

GB-06L.title: Time to Halt Mobilization
GB-06L.event: On 31 July Germany proclaimed a "state of imminent danger of war."
GB-06L.scene: The London conference opens in two days, but mobilization orders are moving faster than diplomacy. Russian mobilization has not stopped, and Moltke says that the moment Russia moves toward the German frontier, Germany will have no choice but to mobilize too. Cambon warns that once German mobilization begins, France will not wait either. You must find a way to halt these movements before the ambassadors sit down at the table.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Berlin says it can wait if Russia halts mobilization on the German frontier alone. But the General Staff says it can hardly hold out more than a day or two.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: If words cannot hold them back, the fleet must show them. Keep the fleet at its North Sea war stations and let it be known that whoever moves first will have Britain to deal with.

choices.text: As Churchill advises, keep the fleet at its North Sea war stations until the conference meets, and warn whoever moves first
choices.why: If words cannot restrain them, the fleet must speak instead
choices.after: At the warning that the British fleet stood ready at its North Sea war stations, the German navy grew tense, and Berlin put off its mobilization order by a day. But Vienna suspected Britain had sided with Russia and resolved to concede nothing at the conference.

choices.text: As Lichnowsky reports, mediate so that Germany delays mobilizing if Russia halts mobilization on the German frontier
choices.why: Freezing mobilization gives the ambassadors time to work
choices.after: Sazonov insisted that mobilization already ordered could not be withdrawn, but agreed that the forces on the German frontier would move no further, and Berlin delayed mobilization while the conference sat. Amid grumbling from both general staffs, the conference was set to open as planned.

note.text: In fact, Germany demanded on 31 July that Russia stop mobilizing within 12 hours, and Germany’s mobilization plan provided for operations into Luxembourg and Belgium almost simultaneously with mobilization.

GB-07L.title: The Ambassadors' Table
GB-07L.scene: As in the conference of ambassadors that handled the aftermath of the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913, the Great Powers' ambassadors have gathered again at the Foreign Office in London. You take the chair, flanked by Lichnowsky of Germany, Cambon of France and the Italian ambassador, while the Austrian and Russian ambassadors wait to be called in separately. Austria demands guarantees of a thorough investigation of the plotting inside Serbia; Russia insists that Serbia’s independence must not be touched. A single line of text could mean war or peace.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Vienna cannot go home empty-handed. It must have some visible pledge.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Russia will not sign a text that cuts into Serbia’s sovereignty, and France cannot abandon Russia.

choices.text: As Lichnowsky asks, accept Austria’s occupation of Belgrade until Serbia has fulfilled its promises
choices.why: Send Vienna home empty-handed and the next crisis will come sooner
choices.after: The Austrian army remained in Belgrade. Russia signed, but the St Petersburg newspapers denounced it as one more humiliation.

choices.text: As Cambon and Benckendorff demand, press for immediate withdrawal and full protection of Serbia, and wait for Vienna to yield
choices.why: If the Entente powers hold firm together, Vienna will back down first
choices.after: Vienna threatened to walk out of the conference, and Berlin hardened, saying it could not abandon its ally. The conference adjourned without a result.

choices.text: Have an international commission supervise Serbia’s inquiry into the plot, and in return have the Austrian army leave Belgrade
choices.why: An agreement lasts only if both sides can save face
choices.after: Austria kept its honor, and Russia kept Serbia. Conrad raged that once again the chance for a preventive war had been lost.

note.text: The London Conference of Ambassadors, which met from December 1912 to August 1913 with Grey in the chair, settled Albanian independence and its frontiers; at the same time the peace conference of the Balkan belligerents met at St James’s Palace.

GB-08LX.title: The Conference Adjourned
GB-08LX.event: On 3 August the London conference of ambassadors adjourned without a result.
GB-08LX.scene: Four days have passed since the conference adjourned. Vienna threatens to quit the conference for good, and Conrad’s army will be ready to advance into Serbia around 12 August. Russia is keeping its partially mobilized forces on the frontier, and Berlin will not give way, saying it cannot abandon its ally. You must decide whether to save the conference or to hold firm to the end with France and Russia.

voices.who: Lichnowsky (German ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: If Vienna goes home empty-handed, Berchtold will fall and Conrad will have his way. Give us just one pledge, and Berlin will hold Vienna back.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Ask Russia to back down again and it will remember the humiliation of 1909. In the next crisis Russia will listen to no one.

choices.text: Heed Cambon and do not make Russia back down again; demand Vienna’s withdrawal to the end, even if the conference collapses
choices.why: A repeat of the 1909 humiliation would bring the entente down
choices.after: On 12 August the Austrian army crossed the Drina, and Russia answered with general mobilization. Germany brought out its western war plan again, and Britain went into the same war alongside France, about ten days later than it did in fact.

choices.text: As Lichnowsky asks, urge Russia to accept Austria’s occupation of Belgrade as a pledge until Serbia keeps its promises
choices.why: If one pledge prevents a great war, it is a cheap bargain
choices.after: Sazonov was furious, but Nicholas II accepted a plan urged by Britain and France together. The conference reopened and signed a text under which the Austrian army would go no farther than Belgrade.

note.text: In reality the Austrian army did cross the Drina into Serbia on 12 August, but in mid-August it was defeated by the Serbian army at the Battle of Cer and fell back.

GB-08L.title: The Price of Peace
GB-08L.scene: In late August, back home at Fallodon for the first time in weeks, you walk in the garden where the birds gather. Your sight is dimmer than before, and you know a distant bird first by its song. In London the Conservatives praise your diplomacy, and Liberal backbenchers are startled to learn how close Britain came to war. But Irish Home Rule is back on the Cabinet table, and the cracks in the alliance system that this crisis exposed remain. Now you must choose how to prevent the next crisis.

voices.who: Nicolson (Permanent Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, gist)
voices.text: We were lucky this time, but deterrence will work next time only if we turn the ententes with France and Russia into a formal alliance.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: We should build on the experience of working with Germany in this crisis. If we slow the naval race, the money can go to social reform.

choices.text: Building on the Conservatives' help during the crisis, push an Irish deal excluding part of Ulster for a fixed period
choices.why: Only by preventing civil war at home can Britain be strong abroad
choices.after: Carrying on the spirit in which they had helped the government during the crisis, the Conservative leaders agreed to the temporary exclusion of part of Ulster. The danger of civil war eased a little.

choices.text: As Nicolson has long urged, turn the ententes with France and Russia into a formal alliance so deterrence works in the next crisis
choices.why: Vague promises bring every crisis to the edge of war
choices.after: France and Russia welcomed it, but Berlin took it as the completion of encirclement. Moltke revived his argument that Germany must fight before Russia finished rearming.

choices.text: As Lloyd George hopes, reopen talks with Germany to slow the naval race, and spend the savings on social reform
choices.why: Trust with Germany must be built into institutions to make crises rarer
choices.after: Naval talks reopened for the first time since Haldane’s failed mission to Berlin in 1912. Cambon worries that Britain is drawing closer to Germany.

note.text: Grey knew birdsong well enough to publish The Charm of Birds in 1927, and in his last years, when he had almost lost his sight, he wrote of the pleasure of recognizing birds by sound alone.

GB-07N.title: The Cost of Neutrality
GB-07N.scene: Since you sent Berlin word that Britain accepts neutrality, the mood at the Foreign Office has turned cold. Nicolson and Crowe have laid their letters of resignation on their desks, while the City, with the Stock Exchange closed, is relieved. In the afternoon Cambon calls. His younger brother, Jules Cambon, is French ambassador in Berlin, so the two brothers are watching this crisis from London and Berlin respectively.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Because of the 1912 agreement on fleet dispositions, France left its northern coast bare. If Britain forgets that, what is France to call its friendship with Britain?

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: A wise decision. Britain is strongest when it stays out of continental wars. The City and our trade will prove it.

choices.text: Grant Cambon the one duty the 1912 fleet arrangement implies: if Germany’s fleet attacks France’s north coast, Britain stops it
choices.why: Even in neutrality, the safety of the Channel is Britain’s own interest
choices.after: Cambon secured at least a minimal promise. Berlin protested that British neutrality was only half a neutrality.

choices.text: As Morley says, spend Britain’s remaining strength on preventing a continental war, and press Paris hard to restrain St Petersburg
choices.why: If France holds Russia back, the war itself may be stopped
choices.after: Paris urged Russia to show restraint, but Russian general mobilization had already begun. That day Germany sent Russia an ultimatum.

choices.text: Having chosen neutrality, hide nothing from Cambon: Britain will not fight for France, so France must decide for itself
choices.why: Raising false hopes would be the greater betrayal
choices.after: Cambon rose without a word. That night the Viviani cabinet in Paris began preparing to fight without Britain.

note.text: Paul Cambon had been French ambassador in London since 1898 and led the way to the Entente Cordiale of 1904, and his younger brother, Jules Cambon, had been French ambassador in Berlin since 1907.

GB-08N.title: The Conservatives' Letter
GB-08N.scene: Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and entered Luxembourg on the morning of 2 August. The Conservative leaders, Bonar Law and Lansdowne, have written to Asquith warning that Britain’s honor and security are at stake if it does not support France and Russia. Churchill says he will stake his post at the Admiralty, and at the Foreign Office Crowe and Nicolson have already resigned. Yet most Liberal backbenchers, the City and the Manchester Guardian support your decision.

voices.who: Bonar Law and Lansdowne (Conservative leaders, letter to Asquith)
voices.text: It would be fatal to the honour and security of the United Kingdom to hesitate in supporting France and Russia at the present juncture.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: If we have chosen neutrality, we must hold to it to the end. But if Belgium is trampled, opinion will turn overnight.

choices.text: As Lloyd George says, stay neutral but publicly demand that Germany not violate Belgium; if it does, neutrality is over
choices.why: Draw a line at Belgium and public opinion will follow the government
choices.after: Berlin did not reply. That evening in Brussels the German minister delivered an ultimatum demanding passage for German troops through Belgium.

choices.text: Hold to neutrality despite the Conservatives' letter, relying on the majority in Parliament, the Liberal backbenches and the City
choices.why: A government cannot lead a war that most of Parliament does not want
choices.after: The Conservatives signaled a motion of no confidence, and Churchill announced his resignation. To keep the Cabinet together, Asquith had to give the Admiralty to someone else.

GB-10N.title: The Neutrality Speech
GB-10N.event: On 2 August Germany demanded passage through Belgium for its troops, and on the morning of 3 August Belgium refused.
GB-10N.scene: You have chosen to keep Britain out of this war. Last night Germany demanded passage through Belgium for its army, and this morning the Belgian government refused. The German embassy has let it be known that Germany will not attack France’s northern coast if Britain stays neutral. The benches are full; the Conservatives are icy and the Liberals uneasy.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: By staying out of Europe’s quarrel, Britain can become the world’s mediator. When the war is over, it will not be the exhausted belligerents who lead the peace conference but the nation that has husbanded its strength.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: Even if we declare neutrality, the fleet must stay mobilized. We must not give the impression that the Royal Navy is sitting idle.

choices.text: As Morley says, declare complete neutrality: this is not Britain’s war, and protecting the City and trade comes first
choices.why: The nation that husbands its strength will lead the peace after the war
choices.after: Liberal backbenchers and the City cheered. But that night Cambon telegraphed Paris that Britain was finished.

choices.text: As Churchill advises, declare armed neutrality: keep the fleet mobilized and state that the duties of the 1839 treaty still stand
choices.why: Even a neutral must show strength, or Germany will treat the treaty lightly
choices.after: The House backed the government’s caution, but the Conservatives attacked it as hypocrisy to speak of treaty obligations without acting on them. The German embassy welcomed Britain’s declaration of neutrality but in the end promised nothing about Belgium.

GB-11N.title: Belgium Invaded
GB-11N.event: On the morning of 4 August German troops crossed the Belgian frontier.
GB-11N.scene: German troops crossed the Belgian frontier at Gemmenich this morning. King Albert I has appealed to the guarantor powers of the 1839 treaty for help, and the first guns are sounding at the forts of Liège. London’s newsboys are crying "Belgium invaded," and in the lobbies of the Commons the Liberal members who backed neutrality yesterday are murmuring. British neutrality rested on the assumption that Germany would not march through Belgium.

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: No Liberal Party can stand by and watch a small nation trampled. Public opinion has already turned.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: Will you send hundreds of thousands of young Britons to the continent for Belgium? A protest and aid are enough.

choices.text: Use the fleet to guard only the Belgian coast and Antwerp, and stay out of the land war with Germany
choices.why: Guard the coast and Germany’s reach will never extend to Britain
choices.after: The British fleet guarded the southern North Sea but stayed out of the war on land. Germany steered clear of the Belgian coast to avoid a clash with Britain.

choices.text: As Morley says, stay neutral: send Germany a note of protest and help Belgian refugees and the wounded
choices.why: A protest and aid alone are enough to save Britain’s face
choices.after: Britain protested but did not move. The Belgian army fell back on Antwerp, and the German right wing poured into northern France.

choices.text: As Lloyd George says, turn around: send Germany an ultimatum and enter the war for Belgium, late as it is
choices.why: Britain cannot stand aside and watch a small nation trampled
choices.after: Britain went to war several days later than it did in fact, and with its Cabinet more badly shaken. France welcomed the decision but never fully trusted Britain.

note.text: As Grey reminded the Commons on 3 August 1914, Gladstone in 1870 held that treaty obligations alone could not settle everything, yet he judged that standing by while Belgium was crushed would be contrary to Britain’s honor and interests.

GB-09E.title: Germany Turns East
GB-09E.scene: On receiving the formal British note, Wilhelm II overrode Moltke’s protests and halted the deployment in the west. Germany promises not to attack France in the west while it fights Russia, and asks Britain to guarantee French neutrality. But under its alliance with Russia, France must fight Germany if Germany attacks Russia. In Paris, Poincaré and Viviani regard the British proposal as a betrayal.

voices.who: Cambon (French ambassador in London, gist)
voices.text: Britain is asking France to abandon Russia. If France abandons its ally, who will trust France after that?

voices.who: Lloyd George (Chancellor of the Exchequer, gist)
voices.text: If Germany does not attack in the west, Britain has no reason to fight either. We must not miss this chance.

choices.text: As Lloyd George says, leave it to France: if it keeps its alliance and attacks Germany, Britain will not enter that war
choices.why: Britain has no cause to fight for someone else’s alliance
choices.after: Paris decided to keep the alliance. French troops began massing on the Lorraine frontier, and the German General Staff brought out its western war plan once more.

choices.text: Ask Poincaré and Viviani not to cross the frontier, and guarantee Britain will join at once if Germany strikes first in the west
choices.why: With a guarantee in hand, France can afford to wait at its frontier
choices.after: After long debate, Paris decided to stay mobilized but not to cross the frontier. Russia was furious that France had betrayed its alliance obligations.

note.text: On 1 August 1914 Wilhelm II did halt the advance in the west for a few hours after Lichnowsky’s telegram arrived, but Moltke objected that the deployment of armies numbering millions could not be changed on the spur of the moment.

GB-10E.title: A Guarantee for the West
GB-10E.scene: You stand before the Commons. In the east Germany and Russia are at war, but the western frontier is still quiet. If Britain guarantees peace on the western frontier, whichever country crosses it first becomes Britain’s enemy. You must make a final choice between friendship with France and Britain’s own safety.

voices.who: Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty, gist)
voices.text: A guarantee means something only with force behind it. Keep the fleet mobilized and declare that we will stop at sea any country that breaks the guarantee.

voices.who: Morley (Lord President of the Council, gist)
voices.text: A guarantee is a promise, and that promise will end in war. Keep Britain’s hands free.

choices.text: As Churchill advises, guarantee peace in the west and declare that the fleet will stop whoever crosses the frontier first
choices.why: Stake the fleet on the guarantee and the western frontier will stay quiet
choices.after: The House backed the government. The two armies facing each other on the western frontier now had to reckon with the British fleet.

choices.text: As Morley says, give no guarantee at all; keep Britain’s hands free and watch how events unfold in the west
choices.why: A guarantee will in the end become a promise of war
choices.after: Without a guarantee the western frontier did not stay quiet for long. A few weeks later the guns sounded in the west as well, and Britain watched from across the sea.

epilogues.A: In August 1914 Grey made his name as the foreign secretary who prevented a European war by leading a second London conference of ambassadors. In the autumn he went back to Fallodon and the Itchen to rest with his fishing and the birdsong, but his sight kept failing. Britain kept the ambiguity of an entente with France that it never turned into an alliance, and no one could say whether that ambiguity would hold in the next crisis. Irish Home Rule and Ulster remained the Cabinet’s greatest problem.
epilogues.B: The Austrian army stayed in Belgrade, and the London conference of ambassadors papered over the Serbian question. Grey was hailed as the mediator who had prevented war, but in Russia resentment grew that Britain had deserted Serbia at the decisive moment, and Anglo-Russian friction over Persia flared up again. At the Foreign Office Crowe wrote a memorandum warning that the entente might survive in name only.
epilogues.C: While Germany and Russia fought in the east, the western frontier stayed quiet, and the British fleet guaranteed that peace. Grey was credited with preventing half of a continental war, but in Paris he was remembered as the man who made France abandon its alliance. At the Foreign Office the worry never faded that if Germany won in the east, its strength would one day turn west.
epilogues.D: Britain watched the continental war from across the sea. The City was relieved for a time, but as German armies took Belgium and northern France, the "friendless England" Crowe had warned of began to come true. Grey left the Foreign Office amid fierce criticism from the Conservatives and the press, and at Fallodon, listening to birdsong with failing eyes, he would ask himself again whether he had chosen rightly.
epilogues.E: Grey remained foreign secretary until Asquith’s government fell in December 1916; that July he had become Viscount Grey of Fallodon. In May 1914 his eye doctors had already told him that he would one day be unable to read; in 1915 he had to rest his eyes for six weeks, and in his last years, almost blind, he recognized birds by their songs. In his 1925 memoir, Twenty-Five Years, he recorded that one evening just before the war (on 3 August, as his friend Spender remembered it), standing at a window of the Foreign Office, he remarked: "The lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our life-time." Until his death at Fallodon in 1933, people argued over whether he had led Britain into the war or had brought a united Britain into a war that could not be avoided.
epilogues.F: The crisis of summer 1914 passed, but the alliance system and the arms race remained. When crisis broke out again a few years later, Germany moved first, and Grey’s successor faced the same question, with fleets larger than in 1914 and the two blocs more firmly set. This ending leaves a question: can a peace that buys time become the preparation for a greater war?

dossier.t: Born in London in 1862 and raised at Fallodon in Northumberland, you are 52 in July 1914. You have been foreign secretary since December 1905; you read French but do not speak it, and you are known as a foreign secretary who almost never travels abroad. In February 1906 you lost your wife, Dorothy, in a carriage accident, and in 1911 your brother George, with whom you had planned one day to live at Fallodon, was killed by a lion in East Africa. You loved trout fishing and birdwatching above all else, published a book on angling, Fly Fishing, in 1899, and on weekends went off to your cottage on the River Itchen in Hampshire. In May 1914 two eye specialists told you that you would one day be unable to read.

Prime Minister Asquith and Lord Chancellor Haldane had been your allies on foreign policy within the Liberal Party since the 1890s, and in the autumn of 1905 the three of you reached an understanding about places in the new government at Relugas, your fishing lodge in Scotland. At the Foreign Office, Permanent Under-Secretary Nicolson and Assistant Under-Secretary Crowe stood firmly for keeping the ententes with Russia and France, and your private secretary, Tyrrell, who handled contacts with the ambassadors, was your closest working aide. In London you rented the house of Churchill, the First Lord of the Admiralty, at 33 Eccleston Square, and during the crisis Churchill would call there late at night to discuss the fleet. The German ambassador, Lichnowsky, and the French ambassador, Cambon, both trusted you, but they were waiting for opposite answers from you.

Your greatest fear is Ireland. The Ulster Volunteers had armed themselves, and in the Curragh incident in March army officers had declared they would rather be dismissed than move against Ulster. The Liberal government depended on the votes of the Irish Nationalists and Labour, and most of the Cabinet opposed involvement in a continental war, so a foreign secretary who committed Britain in advance could bring the government down. Your hope is to prevent war between the Great Powers through a conference of ambassadors in London, as in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913, and you expect the agreements on the Portuguese colonies and the Baghdad Railway, initialed with Germany in 1913 and 1914, to steady relations between the two countries. You had said in the Commons that you were willing to make a new friend, wherever it could be done, without losing an old one.

movers.intro: Whether Grey bears responsibility for leading Britain into the war, or brought a united country into a war that could not be avoided, is an old debate. The main views are these.
views: Niall Ferguson: in The Pity of War (1998), he argues that Grey and the Foreign Office exaggerated the German threat, that without British intervention the continental war would have been shorter and smaller, and that Britain’s entry into the war was a great mistake.

Christopher Clark: criticizes Grey for centering his policy on preserving the ententes without fully informing the Cabinet and Parliament of the military talks with France and Russia, and for sending Germany signals that stayed ambiguous to the end.

Keith Wilson: in The Policy of the Entente (1985), he argues that the central motive of British diplomacy was less to contain Germany than to preserve friendship with Russia, which could threaten Britain in India and Persia.

Thomas Otte: in July Crisis (2014) and his 2020 biography of Grey, he judges Grey’s mediation efforts to have been sincere and holds that the crisis was escalated by Vienna and Berlin’s insistence on a local war, giving Grey a relatively generous verdict.
movers.note: Some have suggested that grief for his wife and his failing eyesight clouded Grey’s judgment in 1914, but many reply that such an influence is hard to demonstrate from the sources.
